## Where was the brewing city before Prohibition?

The breweries around Cincinnati crossed the Ohio River, but they did not spread evenly across the three cities. These thirteen placements gather most tightly around Over-the-Rhine, with Bavarian and Phillip Jung across the river in Covington and Wiedemann in Newport. For Day 6's Vintage theme, the background is the historical document: two USGS topographic sheets labelled 1914, with their street grids, railway lines, contours, ink and paper left visible.

This is a reconstruction from a historical brewery list, not a complete census of businesses open on one date. The Queen City chronology supplies ownership chains and operating periods. Following those chains matters. Ohio Union did not become Cincinnati Home until 1915; Crown inherited the Schmidt Brothers plant in 1904. Hudepohl belongs near Clifton and Frintz here, rather than at a later brewery associated with the name.

## Method

The package experiment is georeferenced historical imagery with `terra`. The scans contain NAD27 American Polyconic definitions, each with its own central meridian. I masked each sheet to its geographic neatline before projecting both to a common six-metre NAD83 / UTM zone 16N grid and mosaicking them. This removes the printed collars without pretending that matching pixel sizes mean matching coordinate systems. The original sheets are 1:62,500; the displayed crop has been resized, so the kilometre bar supplies the usable scale.

Symbols describe the placement method. Circles represent an address reduced to a block midpoint. Diamonds use an OSM building associated with the historical complex. Triangles use a street intersection named in the chronology, sometimes through a predecessor firm. Every point is a site proxy, not a surveyed entrance or parcel. The Bavarian placement uses the surviving government-center building, with its brewery connection checked against the family's exhibit history.

The [acquisition script](acquire-data.R) downloads and fingerprints the sources, writes the [brewery reduction](breweries.csv), and prepares the mosaic. The [renderer](render-map.R) works offline. [Location decisions](location-decisions.csv) retain the OSM identifiers and the reasoning behind each coordinate; the [source snapshot](source-snapshot.json) records SHA-256 values and both embedded CRS definitions.

## Data & provenance

No city directory was used. Historical locations and operation dates come from the [Queen City Chapter chronology](https://queencitychapter.com/brewinghistory/preprohibition.htm). Modern coordinates come from [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright), under the Open Database License. The [Bavarian exhibit history](https://www.pinemeer.org/copy-of-special-museums) connects the surviving building to its earlier use. Sources were retrieved November 11, 2026; the post date follows the challenge day.

An asterisk means the firm is named in the [1903 *One Hundred Years of Brewing*](https://archive.org/details/onehundredyearso0000vari_c0n2). I checked names in local context, rather than counting every “Bavarian” or “Gambrinus” in the OCR. A missing asterisk is not evidence of closure, and a match proves neither a 1914 address nor uninterrupted operation.

The USGS [West Cincinnati](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/StagedProducts/Maps/HistoricalTopo/GeoTIFF/OH/OH_West%20Cincinnati_709982_1914_62500_geo.tif) and [East Cincinnati](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/StagedProducts/Maps/HistoricalTopo/GeoTIFF/OH/OH_East%20Cincinnati_708568_1914_62500_geo.tif) scans are [public domain](https://www.usgs.gov/information-policies-and-instructions/copyrights-and-credits). Their edition labels do not guarantee that every printed feature was surveyed in 1914. Historical prose remains with its respective rights holders; the reduction records facts and source links.

## What I learned

The hardest join was between a historical address and a modern street. Herancourt, Schaller, Foss-Schneider, Lackman, Bruckmann, Wetterer, Mohawk, Fairmont, Cincinnati's Jung Western and Adam remain off the map because I could not resolve their sites from these extracts. The [exclusion table](excluded-firms.csv) says why. A familiar brewery name on a modern building is a lead to investigate, not permission to move the old brewery there.

**Alt text:** Thirteen brewery-site proxies over historical topographic scans of Cincinnati, Covington and Newport; numbered symbols distinguish placement evidence, with a firm key below.
